title: k nearest neighbours
story:
Every other method in this track commits in advance to a shape. A line, a logistic curve, a partition into rectangles, a weighted sum of trees — each says something about the form the relationship takes before seeing whether it does. This one refuses to commit. Keep the examples; to classify a new point, look at the nearest recorded points and report what they were.

Fix and Hodges defined the rule in 1951, in a technical report for the USAF School of Aviation Medicine at Randolph Field, on nonparametric discrimination and its consistency properties. The word nonparametric is the whole claim: there are no parameters, because there is no assumed form to have parameters about.

Cover and Hart worked out what that buys, in 1967, and the result is one of the more surprising in the subject. The rule is, as they put it, independent of the underlying joint distribution on the sample points and their classifications — it assumes nothing. And yet in the large-sample limit its error is bounded: for any number of categories, the probability of error of the nearest neighbour rule is bounded above by twice the Bayes probability of error. Their gloss is the line to remember — in this sense it may be said that half the classification information in an infinite sample set is contained in the nearest neighbour.

Sit with how strong that is. The Bayes error is the floor, the error of a rule that knows the true probability structure exactly. Looking at one neighbour, assuming nothing, gets you within a factor of two of a rule that knows everything. Half the available information is in the single closest example.

Now the conditions, because the bound is asymptotic and the conditions are where real use lives. It holds in the limit of infinite data, and says nothing about the sample you have. It depends entirely on the distance function, which you chose — so it inherits every scaling decision, and a feature measured in thousands dominates one measured in fractions for no reason but its units. And nearness degrades with dimension: as the number of features grows, distances between points concentrate, the nearest neighbour becomes barely nearer than the furthest, and the rule's premise quietly dissolves while the code continues to run.

The practical costs are the inverse of everything else here. There is no training, and prediction is expensive because the work was deferred rather than done. The whole dataset has to be kept, so the model is the data. The method that assumes least demands most at the moment you use it.

problem.name: Nonparametric neighbourhood classification
problem.shape: A prediction is needed for a new point and there is no reason to believe the relationship takes any particular functional form.
tell: the decision boundary is expected to be irregular
the dataset is small enough to keep and search
features are on incomparable scales and a distance is about to be computed
problem.move: Keep the examples and classify by the labels of the nearest ones, choosing the neighbourhood size to trade noise against locality. Scale the features first, since the distance treats units as importance, and check the number of dimensions, because the whole idea depends on nearest meaning something.
problem.invariant: In the large-sample limit the error of the single nearest neighbour rule is at most twice the Bayes error, whatever the underlying distribution — so half the classification information in an infinite sample is carried by the closest example.
problem.breaks: The guarantee is asymptotic and the premise is geometric. As dimensionality grows, distances between points concentrate and the nearest neighbour stops being meaningfully nearer than the rest, so the rule degrades to guessing while continuing to return answers with no indication that its premise has failed.

cost.time: no training at all, and prediction that scales with the size of the dataset unless an index is built — the work is deferred, not avoided
cost.space: the entire training set is the model and must be retained and shipped
cost.beats: parametric methods when no form is defensible, and loses to them whenever a defensible form exists, since assuming a true shape is worth more than assuming none

worked.problem: What does the bound of twice the Bayes error actually promise?
worked.reasoning:
Something remarkable, under conditions that are easy to lose sight of.

The promise first. The Bayes error is the floor — the error rate of a rule that knows the true joint distribution exactly and is therefore unbeatable. The result says that in the large-sample limit, the single nearest neighbour rule has an error rate at most twice that floor, for any number of categories, and the rule attains this while being independent of the underlying joint distribution. Assuming nothing about the shape of the problem, looking at exactly one stored example, you land within a factor of two of omniscience. Their own gloss is that half the classification information in an infinite sample set is contained in the nearest neighbour.

Now the conditions, which are three and all matter.

It is asymptotic. It describes behaviour as the sample grows without bound, and says nothing about the dataset in front of you. With finite data the nearest neighbour is not close, and the guarantee does not apply.

It is relative. Twice a small number is small; twice a large number is large. If the Bayes error for your problem is thirty percent, the bound permits sixty, which is not a useful promise. The result bounds the ratio to the best achievable, not the absolute error.

And it depends on the distance, which is not given by the problem. Nearest means nearest under a metric you selected, so every scaling decision is a modelling decision — a feature in thousands will dominate one in fractions purely because of its units. The theorem assumes the geometry is meaningful; it cannot supply that.

The failure mode I would raise unprompted is dimensionality. As the number of features grows, pairwise distances concentrate: the nearest point becomes barely nearer than the furthest, so the neighbourhood stops being local in any useful sense. The rule keeps returning answers, with no signal that the premise underneath it has dissolved. That is why this method is strong on low-dimensional problems with plenty of data, and why it is usually the wrong reach on wide ones.

So what the bound promises is that the method is not naive — there is real theory saying it recovers half the available information — and what it does not promise is anything about a finite, high-dimensional, unscaled dataset, which is the usual case.

problem.practice: Take a dataset with a handful of features and record the ratio of the distance to the nearest neighbour against the distance to the furthest. Then append fifty columns of pure noise and compute the same ratio again. Watch it approach one, and note that the classifier will report predictions either way.

beats.broke: Fitting a model means committing in advance to the form the relationship must take, and sometimes no particular form is defensible.
beats.fix: Fit nothing. Keep the examples and classify a new point by the labels of the nearest recorded ones — a rule that is independent of the underlying joint distribution and assumes nothing about the boundary's shape.
beats.cost: The training cost moves to prediction time and the whole dataset must be retained, and nearest depends entirely on a distance you chose, which makes scaling and dimensionality decisive rather than incidental.

interview.q: What does the bound of twice the Bayes error actually promise?
interview.trap: Quoting it as a guarantee about your model. It is asymptotic, it bounds the ratio to the best achievable rather than the absolute error, and it presumes a distance function that you supplied — none of which survives a finite, unscaled, high-dimensional dataset.
interview.answer:
Something genuinely remarkable, under three conditions that are easy to forget.

The promise: the Bayes error is the floor, the rate of a rule that knows the true joint distribution exactly and cannot be beaten. In the large-sample limit the single nearest neighbour rule has error at most twice that floor, for any number of categories, while being independent of the underlying distribution. Assuming nothing and looking at one stored example puts you within a factor of two of omniscience — half the classification information in an infinite sample sits in the nearest neighbour.

The conditions. It is asymptotic: it describes behaviour as the sample grows without bound and says nothing about the data in front of you. It is relative: twice a small number is small, twice a large one is large, so with a Bayes error of thirty percent the bound permits sixty, which promises little. And it depends on a distance function the problem does not supply, so every scaling decision becomes a modelling decision — a feature measured in thousands dominates one measured in fractions purely by units.

The failure I would raise unprompted is dimensionality. As features multiply, pairwise distances concentrate until the nearest point is barely nearer than the furthest, so the neighbourhood stops being local in any useful sense. The rule keeps returning answers with no indication that its premise has dissolved, which is why this works well on low-dimensional problems with plenty of data and is usually the wrong reach on wide ones.

So the bound promises that the method is principled rather than naive, and promises nothing about a finite, unscaled, high-dimensional dataset — which is the usual case.

   and scale the features FIRST.
takeaway: Looking at the single nearest example gets within twice the best achievable error while assuming nothing at all — but that is an asymptotic promise about a ratio, under a distance you chose, and it dissolves quietly as dimensions grow.
